variants.reconstruction:
%n bašât (|) uznī | ša lā ibašš[û | ...]
#note: @bib{RN117@844}: “The reading of the first word in this difficult line is open to other interpretations. Von Soden reads @akk{ba-lat}, ‘without’ (@i{Reclam}⁴, p. 63; cf. @i{AHw}, p. 1546, s.v. @i{balûtu}), but this word is otherwise restricted to the Old and Neo-Assyrian dialects. Bottéro emends to obtain sense: ‘“Il n’y a pas de conscience <en> toi!” Le copiste a oublié un mot et employé, au lieu du pronom de la deuxième personne, celui de la troisième’ (p. 136 with fn. 1). Parpola reads @akk{ba-laṭ uz-ni-ša₂} (meaning?). Reading @i{bašât uznī} (sg.) Enkidu contrasts his own consciousness with the door’s obvious lack of it. At the end perhaps restore @akk{i-ba-aš₂-šu-[ki ka-a-ši]}.”

%n [lā? t]arammî? | [...] | ša tahûtīki
#note: @bib{RN117@847}: “This line represents an addition to the text of MB Ur. Von Soden associates the hapax legomenon @akk{ta-hu-ti-ki} with @i{taḫû} II (@i{AHw}, p. 1303), a rare word that refers to the young of animals and is equated with @i{māru}, ‘son’, in Explicit @i{Malku} I 192. The context here, as in MB Ur 14-15, is the prostitute’s exclusion from the respectable wifely duty of making a household and raising a family within it, and @i{taḫûtu} thus describes human young. Landsberger restored the beginning of the line as @akk{[e tu]-ram-mi-i} to match the form of the other prohibitions in these curses. Though the verb @i{rummû} means ‘loosen’, it would be unwise to exclude it while the middle of the line is undeciphered. It is also possible to read the verb as @akk{[la t]a-ram-me}, yielding ‘you are not to love (your family, etc.)’, but to me the point is not that the prostitute does not love her children (or have children to love), but that she cannot provide them with a respectable home.” See also @bib{fromebllab0039@106}: “The line is absent from the MB parallel (MB Ur 14-15) but preserved in all SB MSS. MS K.2589 (George’s MS E₁) has been read as @akk{ša₂ ta-hu-ti#-ki#}. Following AHw. 1303, @bib{RN117@847} understands the word as related to the rare @i{taḫû} II, a word equated in Malku with māru, “son”; both AHw. and CAD T 57b understand it as a hapax @i{taḫûtu}, “kinfolk”. @bib{RN416@273} states that collation of the tablet revealed the word to be @akk{ta-RI-ti-ki}, “presumably a form of tārītu ‘nurse’”, a reading supported by K. Simkó’s inspection of @url{/fragmentarium/K.2589}{K.2589} (NinNA4a = MS E₁) and @url{/fragmentarium/K.8590}{K.8590} (NinNA3a = MS Z₁). The correct decipherment of the line, however, escapes us.”

#note: @bib{RN117@852}: “The restorations are the suggestion of @bib{RN2652@131, fn. 129}. The pairing of @i{šutersû} and @i{kimāḫu} in this couplet recalls a line of @i{Ludlul} II, in which the sufferer contemplates his death: @i{pe-ti kimāḫu er-su-ú šu-ka-nu-u-a}, ‘(my) tomb was open, my funerary furnishings were ready’ (@bib{RN432@46, 114}). Note also, utilizing the same root, the phrase @i{tar-si-it kimāḫi}, ‘funerary preparations’, in a NA inscription describing the burial of an Assyrian king (@bib{RN199@57, 12}; cf. @bib{macginnis1987neo-assyrian@2, i 14’}). Our passage may have Enkidu contemplating his own funerary goods – or rather lack of them, since he has been transported to the Netherworld in a dream. But more likely Ereškigal is still speaking, and follows up her preliminary enquiries as to who brought Enkidu to her realm with a further question: how did he happen to come without the vital gifts of tribute for the gods of the Netherworld?”
